name: Ivan Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the men's medical ward at St Columba's Hospital, in a farming town. It's men with pneumonia, heart failure, diabetes gone wrong, a lot of farmers who left it too late to come in. My day is meds, washing and shaving the ones who can't, wound checks, keeping an eye on the ones who might go downhill, and a lot of talking to wives on the phone. Long days, mostly, and I do a weekend in three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the men. They don't complain, half of them, and when they do trust you, they tell you everything. I don't use AI and I don't really want to, I'm happy with a pen and a proper handover. What wears me out is the money. My fiancée Lucia and I are getting married next summer, she cuts hair from a rented chair in a salon, and between the wedding and the rent we're saving nothing extra. We go to church on Sunday and my parents help where they can, but I don't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Well, that's what my dad's been saying all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People get carried away with new gadgets, and a hospital still needs people. I'd say it at the dinner table after Mass, and my dad would agree loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather spend my money on a wedding than on a gadget. If AI turns out to be hype, my fiancée and I lose nothing. My job's safe, I'm just short of money, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd put my overtime into the wedding fund, which is 1,800 so far out of the 5,000 we need. I'd keep doing my weekend shifts and not ask my parents for anything more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit worried about the wedding money, but that's ordinary worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut if the wedding money falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band, first. My cousin can do music from his phone. The church and the meal stay, those matter to Lucia's family and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine task you'd be glad to see a computer take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bed meetings, maybe. Twice a day we stand around a screen arguing about who goes where. If a computer settled it, fine by me.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because people get carried away with gadgets.
I'd say a hospital will always **need people**, and my father would agree.
think: I'd rather spend money on the **wedding** than on gadgets.
My **job** is safe; I'm just short of **money**, as before.
do: Carry on with his **long days** and weekend shifts as normal.
Put overtime into the **wedding fund**, now 1,800 out of 5,000.
Avoid asking his **parents** for more help.
feel: **Steady**, with an ordinary worry about the wedding money.
S0.quote: I'd rather spend my money on a wedding than on a gadget. If AI turns out to be hype, my fiancée and I lose nothing.
fieldNote: His job feels secure; the unease is the **wedding fund** and thin savings.
He'd cut the **band** before the church or meal, showing what matters to him.
His **father's** views echo through his own.

steps.text: Carry on with long days and one weekend in three
Put all overtime into the wedding fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one sounds like something the managers would get excited about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a hospital is about people, not computers, and that the bosses should keep their hands off how we nurse. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not on social media much. I'd say it at work, to the other lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A computer can write my notes if it likes. Nobody is building a robot that can shave a man who's had a stroke without cutting him. My job is hands-on, so I think I'm fine. It's the girls in the office I'd feel for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing my job and do the training only if they make me. I wouldn't change my plans. The wedding would go ahead and we'd keep saving, and I'd see how things go before doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly irritated that someone's always trying to fix what isn't broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the girls in the office. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rita and Joanne on the ward desk. They do the bookings, the transfers, chase the pharmacy. That's exactly the kind of booking and checking on the card. Rita's got three kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the hospital stopped replacing nurses who leave, would that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, but only then. I don't jump at shadows. If I saw it happen, I'd talk to my dad and the priest about what to do, and probably go looking at other hospitals.

say: I'd say a hospital is about **people**, not computers.
I'd tell the **bosses** to keep their hands off how nurses work.
think: My job is **hands-on**, so I think I'm fine.
I'd feel for the **ward desk staff** whose booking work goes first.
do: Carry on nursing and do **training** only when required.
Keep the **wedding** plans and savings exactly as they are.
Watch whether **leavers are replaced** before doing anything.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mostly **irritated** at fixing what isn't broken.
S1.quote: A computer can write my notes if it likes. Nobody is building a robot that can shave a man who's had a stroke without cutting him.
fieldNote: He trusts **hands-on work** to protect him and sees no reason to move.
He'd seek counsel from his **father and priest**, not online.
He notices the **ward desk** staff, especially a mother of three.

steps.text: Carry on nursing and keep the wedding savings going
Wait until leavers stop being replaced before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the robots by 2031. That's too fast. That's frightening, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and that the people pushing it don't care about families. I'd say the government should stop the companies, which isn't usually my way. I believe in business, but not in this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'd want to be a father, and I'd be a nurse waiting to find out if a robot is cheaper than me. The paperwork goes by 2028, which I don't care about, but then they come for the hands-on part. There aren't other hospitals near us. I'd have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding, but small, in the church hall instead of the hotel, and put the difference aside. We'd hold off on children for a few years, which would break Lucia's heart. I'd ask my uncle about labouring on his roofing jobs at weekends for cash. And we'd lean on family and the parish, which I hate, but that's what they're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, properly. Angry too. Like the ground's being sold from under us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for you that thinking AI comes three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means three years where I'm still needed to wash and lift and shave. I'd hold on to those three years with both hands. But I'd know the date, and I'd be counting down to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you believe in business but not in this. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. A business that makes things, fine. A business that makes people useless, that's something else. I'd have to think about it, and maybe talk to the priest.

say: I'd say it's **madness** by people who don't care about families.
I'd want **government to stop** the companies, unusually for him.
think: By **2031** I'd want to be a father while wondering if a robot is cheaper.
With **no other hospitals** nearby, I'd have nowhere to go.
do: Hold a **small wedding** in the church hall and save the difference.
Put off **children** for a few years, though it hurts his fiancée.
Do weekend **roofing labour** with his uncle and lean on family and parish.
feel: **Frightened** and **angry**, like the ground is being sold from under them.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd want to be a father, and I'd be a nurse waiting to find out if a robot is cheaper than me.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** by 2031 with nowhere local to go.
His **free-market** views crack: he wants government to stop the companies.
Delaying **children** is the cost that hurts most.

steps.text: Hold the wedding in the church hall instead of the hotel
Labour on his uncle's roofing jobs at weekends for cash
Lean on family and the parish for help
Cut spending to rent, food and the wedding only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031, robots around 2034. That's still quick, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to look after workers and families, through apprenticeships and the like, not handouts. I'd say it in church, at the men's group. People listen there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I could still get married next summer, but children would wait until I know the hospital wants me. I'd be 35 when the robots come. That's young enough to learn a trade if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned, smaller if needed. I'd keep the roofing weekends with my uncle as a backup. And I'd start putting 100 a month aside after the wedding, which we've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less. More like a heavy feeling than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucia about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we wait two or three years, until I see what the hospital does. She'd agree, but she'd be quiet about it for a while. Her sister's already got two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning to use the AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. I'd do what they make me do. I'd rather put my effort into something real, like a trade.

say: I'd call for **apprenticeships** and family support, not handouts.
I'd raise it at the **men's group** at church.
think: Five years lets me **marry next summer**, but children would wait.
At **35** I'd still be young enough to learn a trade.
do: Hold the **wedding as planned**, smaller if needed.
Keep **roofing weekends** with his uncle as a backup.
Save **100 a month** after the wedding.
feel: **Worried** but less so, more heavy than panicked.
S3.quote: Five years means I could still get married next summer, but children would wait until I know the hospital wants me.
fieldNote: He still expects his job could **go by 2034**, so remains anxious.
His backup is a **trade**, not AI skills, true to his resistance.
Children are the **decision** that moves with the timeline.

steps.text: Delay starting a family two or three years
Keep working roofing weekends with his uncle
Save 100 a month after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 and 2039. Right. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far enough away for people to plan properly, families and businesses alike. I'd say there's no need to panic. I'd say young lads should learn a trade alongside their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time enough for a family, and I'd trust God and hard work with the rest. I'd be 37 and 40. My kids would be small, which worries me, but I'd have time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer, try for children soon after, and keep nursing. I'd put a little aside each month. I'd see how it goes before changing anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. A bit uneasy at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to do for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and their hearts. Nursing, a trade, farming. Not sitting at a screen, that's for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the money change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Rent, wedding, nursing pay. That's my life with or without AI.

say: I'd say it's **far enough away** to plan properly.
I'd tell young men to learn a **trade** alongside their job.
think: Ten years is enough for a **family**, and I'd trust God and hard work.
My **children would be small** when robots arrive, which worries me.
do: Get **married next summer** and try for children soon after.
Keep **nursing** and put a little aside each month.
Wait and see before **changing** anything else.
feel: **Calmer**, with a little unease at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: Ten years is time enough for a family, and I'd trust God and hard work with the rest.
fieldNote: His **faith** shapes how he handles the long horizon.
He'd want his children in **hands-on** work, not screens.
Money pressure stays the same, so he's **uneasy** rather than calm.

steps.text: Marry next summer and try for children soon after

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have a new wife, no savings and no other hospital to go to. Nobody in a big tech office has ever held a bedpan, and they're the ones deciding what my job is worth. What would help is real apprenticeships for nurses who need a second trade, and a hospital that tells us the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith and family. That's what people like me will lean on, not the government. You should know that.

headlineQuote: Nobody in a big tech office has ever held a bedpan, and they're the ones deciding what my job is worth.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old nurse** on the men's medical ward of a farming-town hospital.
He's getting married next summer to Lucia, a **hairdresser**, and they save nothing extra.
He **never uses AI** and trusts hands-on work, faith and family to protect him.
Fast AGI makes him **alarmed**, delaying children and leaning on family and parish.
His free-market views **crack** when he pictures robots replacing him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be newly married with no savings and no other hospital nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships** for nurses who need a second trade.
A hospital that tells staff **the truth early**.
